sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions
teaching: An **oscillation** is repeated movement around equilibrium, the resting position. A stretched or compressed spring pulls or pushes the mass back toward that position. The mass has **inertia**, so it keeps moving through equilibrium. The spring is then displaced the other way and brings it back again.

In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves along the spring. In **transverse motion**, it moves across the spring line. The transverse segments are already pulled tight. Moving the mass above or below their resting line changes the direction of their pull, giving a force back toward the line.

The return force and the continued movement play different roles. If the mass is on one side of equilibrium, the spring acts toward equilibrium from that side. After the mass crosses, the spring’s displacement reverses and so does the restoring direction. The back-and-forth pattern comes from this repeated interaction, rather than from a force that always points the same way. The longitudinal and transverse pictures change how that return is arranged, while keeping the same basic relationship between movement and restoring action.

Both examples repeat at the same **frequency**, or number of cycles per unit of time, because their masses and total restoring stiffness are matched. Direction alone does not set the rate. These ideal examples have no damping, so the movement continues instead of gradually dying away.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate
teaching: **Greater mass lowers frequency** when stiffness stays the same. A heavier mass is harder to speed up, slow down, and turn around. The same restoring action therefore takes longer to complete each back-and-forth cycle.

**Greater stiffness raises frequency** when mass stays the same. The same displacement produces a stronger force toward equilibrium, so the mass turns around more quickly and completes more cycles in the same time. Mass changes the resistance to changing motion; stiffness changes the strength of the return.

Each comparison keeps one property unchanged so that the cause of the rate change is clear. The heavier-mass example repeats the same kind of motion but completes fewer cycles than its reference. The stiffer example completes more. A larger visible movement would concern amplitude, or how far the mass travels, rather than establishing a faster rate. To identify frequency, follow complete repetitions over the same interval instead of judging which picture is tallest or which way the mass moves.

The longitudinal and transverse examples match within each comparison because their masses and **effective restoring stiffnesses** match. Effective stiffness means the restoring action in the actual direction of movement. Across the spring line, this depends on tension and arrangement. Making a spring harder to stretch along its length does not automatically increase its transverse restoring action.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes
teaching: Two equal masses connected between fixed ends have **two normal modes**. A normal mode is a coordinated pattern that repeats at one frequency, with the parts maintaining a particular relationship.

In **Mode 1**, both masses move in the same direction together. Their separation changes little, so the middle connection changes relatively little. In **Mode 2**, they move against each other, strongly compressing and stretching that connection. The stronger restoring action makes Mode 2 faster. Its frequency is higher, without necessarily being exactly twice Mode 1’s frequency.

In Mode 1, the masses can travel while keeping nearly the same distance between them. In Mode 2, their distance repeatedly shrinks and grows. That difference explains why the middle connection matters more in the faster pattern, even though the physical masses and connections have not been replaced. A mode describes the relationship across the whole system. It does not mean that one mass belongs to the first mode and the other belongs to the second; both masses participate in each pattern.

Both modes can contribute to the same masses at once. Their movements add at each mass, reinforcing in the same direction and canceling partly or completely in opposite directions. This addition is **superposition**. The combined motion contains both frequencies. The longitudinal and transverse versions preserve these relationships while changing the direction of movement.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes
teaching: Three equal masses between fixed ends have **three normal modes**. In **Mode 1**, all move in the same direction, but the middle mass moves farthest. Moving together therefore does not require equal distances. This is the lowest-frequency pattern.

In **Mode 2**, the outer masses move oppositely while the middle mass stays at equilibrium because the pulls on it balance. That stationary location is a **node**. In **Mode 3**, the outer masses move together against the middle mass. Neighboring parts oppose one another more strongly, making this the fastest pattern.

The order follows how the masses move relative to their neighbors. Mode 1 keeps their broad movement together. Mode 2 makes the outer masses oppose one another but leaves the middle balanced. Mode 3 makes the middle oppose both outer masses, strongly changing their connecting links. These are different arrangements of movement in the same system, not a progression in which an extra mass starts moving at each stage. The colors track the individual masses and the resting marks show what each displacement is measured from.

The frequencies belong to this chain and are not necessarily one, two, and three times the lowest. When the modes combine, their movements add at each mass. The center can move through contributions from Modes 1 and 3 even though it is a node in Mode 2. The same relationships appear in the matched longitudinal and transverse models.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: Each movable mass adds one independent **normal mode** in the direction being modeled. The chains with one through six masses therefore have one through six modes. The empty spaces mark modes that smaller chains do not have, giving 21 displayed comparisons altogether.

Within a chain, **Mode 1** has the broadest pattern, with the masses moving together. Higher modes introduce more groups moving in opposite directions. The connections undergo stronger relative changes, and the patterns repeat faster. Fixed endpoints remain still; a stationary mass inside one mode does not mean the whole chain has stopped.

Within each chain, the masses and connections are equal and both outer supports remain fixed. Changing the mode changes how those same parts move in relation to one another. A higher pattern has more reversals across the chain, so neighboring parts pull against one another in more places. This explains the faster restoring pattern without claiming that a higher mode uses smaller masses or physically stronger replacement springs. Mode number identifies the pattern, not the identity of a particular moving mass.

Colors identify mode number, while each row identifies the number of masses. The largest movements are scaled to the same displayed size, so height cannot establish which mode is faster. **Amplitude** is movement size; frequency is repetition rate. These separate-mass chains generally lack the exact whole-number frequency spacing of an ideal continuous string.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: A **fixed–fixed string** stays still at both endpoints, which are nodes. Mode 1 fits one half-wave into its length; Modes 2–5 fit two through five. More half-waves mean shorter wavelengths and faster repetition at the same wave speed. These frequencies are consecutive **harmonics**, including odd and even multiples of the fundamental.

The same string can contain all five modes. Their movements add at each position, reinforcing or canceling as their cycles progress. The combined outline changes even though the component patterns remain regular. Playback slows all modes equally, preserving their relative rates.

The displayed components are 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz. These labels identify their repetition rates, whereas the half-wave count identifies their shapes along the string. As the mixture moves, a position can become nearly flat through cancellation and later move strongly as the contributions change. This does not mean that a component frequency has been destroyed and replaced. The measured motion still combines the original patterns, with each contribution depending on how that particular mode moves the pickup location.

The marked **pickup** measures movement at one point. Its spectrum places frequency horizontally and amplitude vertically. The five peaks correspond to the five components. Their heights are equal because the mode strengths were chosen to give equal contributions at this pickup; another position can give different heights. Equal peaks do not mean equal movement everywhere.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A **membrane** moves across a surface with fixed outside edges. Its two-number labels count moving regions along the two surface directions. (1,1) has one broad region; (2,1) and (1,2) divide it in different directions; (2,2) makes four regions; and (3,1) makes three along one direction. Neighboring regions move oppositely, separated by stationary nodes.

The five movements add at every point. Contributions can reinforce or cancel, producing one changing surface. The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale, so its apparent height cannot be compared directly with the individual panels.

A node stays still throughout that mode’s cycle. A moving region can also pass briefly through the resting surface, but that momentary crossing does not make it a node. The distinction matters when reading an animation from one frame. Follow the same region as it rises, crosses rest, and falls while its neighbor moves oppositely. The two numbers describe divisions across the surface, rather than two separate frequencies, two different membranes, or a count of cycles that have already elapsed.

The pickup records one location. The spectrum gives frequency horizontally and relative amplitude vertically. The component strengths were chosen to make equal peaks there. Frequencies of 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz were **assigned for the illustration**, rather than calculated as this rectangle’s natural resonances. Their equal spacing demonstrates combining frequencies; it does not establish that every membrane naturally has harmonic spacing.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction
teaching: A **scientific theory** explains a system precisely enough to make a testable prediction. Differential equations describe how its quantities change. Their purpose here is to connect the proposed mechanism with an observable result, rather than to provide a calculation exercise.

The proposed theory treats the **vocal folds as a vibrating membrane**. It predicts **equidistant harmonics** in a laryngeal vibration signal: frequency peaks separated by equal intervals. Testing it requires recording actual laryngeal vibration and examining its spectrum. Regular spacing would agree with the prediction; a different pattern would question the model’s account of that signal.

The proposed observation is more specific than simply seeing movement. The vocal folds could vibrate while the measured frequencies fail to follow the predicted equal spacing. Examining the spectrum connects the theory with the particular feature it predicts. The animation demonstrates what an assigned collection of frequencies looks like when combined; a recording asks whether an actual vocal-fold signal has the proposed pattern. Keeping those roles separate distinguishes an illustration of an idea from evidence obtained by testing that idea.

The material proposes this experiment without reporting a measured outcome. The membrane animation uses assigned harmonic frequencies, so replaying that illustration is not an independent test of natural vocal-fold vibration.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A **fixed–free system** must have a node at the fixed end and an **antinode**, a place of maximum movement, at the free end. The simplest pattern fits one quarter-wave. The next patterns fit three, five, and seven quarter-waves, giving the first, third, fifth, and seventh harmonics. Mode 2 is therefore the third harmonic, not the second.

Odd quarter-wave counts preserve the different endpoint conditions. Even counts would put a node at the free end. Higher patterns fit shorter wavelengths into the same length and repeat faster. The mixture’s spectrum gives frequency horizontally and amplitude vertically. Equal excitation produces equal peaks at the free-end pickup; uniformly slowed playback preserves the relative rates.

An antinode is a place with the greatest movement over a cycle, not a point that stays at its farthest position. It passes through rest and moves to the other side while the fixed endpoint remains still. The illustrated frequencies are 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz. The second, third, and fourth allowed modes are consequently the third, fifth, and seventh harmonics. Counting allowed shapes and comparing their frequencies answer different questions, even though both descriptions use numbers.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were **separately tuned** to the same fundamental. Changing only one endpoint while keeping length and wave speed unchanged would halve the fundamental. Matching displayed labels therefore does not isolate the endpoint’s effect.

Dynamic systems in economic stabilization
teaching: A **dynamic system** changes over time as its parts influence one another. Woodford’s **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or DSGE, is the theory named in the economic example. Economics provides another setting for explaining fluctuations and considering how to reduce harmful extremes.

In the stabilization illustration, the **black curve represents unemployment** and the **gray curve inflation**. Large, jagged peaks and troughs become smaller and smoother. Stabilization means reducing those swings, rather than stopping all change or turning the two quantities into the same thing.

The connection with physical systems is the concern with what produces a fluctuation and what can reduce it. Here, the practical aim is to avoid extremes such as high unemployment or runaway inflation. The changing curves illustrate that aim without supplying a measured test of a particular policy.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: Air has **inertia**, so moving air tends to keep moving. Compression produces a restoring effect, represented by the model’s spring-like links. The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube, rather than traveling steadily from the glottis to the lips.

The glottal end is treated as fixed and the open lips as free. **Mode 1 is F1-like**, the lowest resonance pattern; **Mode 2 is F2-like**, with another internal reversal. In the ideal uniform reference, Mode 2 repeats three times as fast. A changed tract shape can alter that simple relationship.

A resonance pattern describes the air system’s coordinated back-and-forth movement. F1 and F2 do not identify two separate streams or two positions from which sound is emitted. At one location, neighboring elements may move together while their gaps hardly change. At another, the gaps may repeatedly close and open. A constriction acts on both modes at the same physical place, but their different movement and compression patterns give the changed region a different role in each.

The /a/ marker is about one-third of the distance from the glottis, /i/ about two-thirds, and /u/ at the lips. Each marks the same place in both modes. Added mass matters where a mode moves strongly; increased springiness matters where it compresses strongly. Comparing these local roles explains why one narrowing can affect F1 and F2 differently.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction
teaching: **Tongue height** and **front–back position** describe vowel articulation. The vowel in **dean** is high and front, with its marked narrowing about two-thirds of the way from the glottis to the lips. **Dune** is high and back, with a highlighted narrowing at the lips. Sharing tongue height does not give them the same tract shape.

**Dan** is low and front; **Don** is low and back, with its narrowing marked about one-third of the distance from the glottis. **Done** is central and labeled “No constriction,” providing the relatively unconstricted reference. Dan has no numbered narrowing position.

The labels describe related but different features. High versus low concerns tongue height; front versus back concerns its position along the mouth; the marked fraction concerns distance along the air path. A shared label such as high therefore leaves other shape differences open. Dean and dune can both be high while narrowing different places, and those places can play different roles in the second resonance pattern. Describing articulation identifies what changed physically; comparing the air modes explains what that change does to the sound.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples were **separately tuned** to the same fundamental. Changing only one endpoint while keeping length and wave speed unchanged would halve the fundamental. Matching displayed labels therefore does not isolate the endpoint’s effect.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes
teaching: A **quarter-wavelength** connects a node with an antinode. One quarter-wave fits between the stationary fixed bottom and moving free top, giving the simplest allowed pattern without an internal node.

Adding another quarter-wave would end at a node, which is wrong for the free top. Adding two preserves an antinode there. The allowed patterns therefore fit **one, three, five, and seven quarter-waves** into the same length. More sections mean shorter wavelengths and faster repetition at unchanged wave speed.

The numbered pieces divide the standing-wave shape. They do not move sequentially up the string. The material moves back and forth while the pattern’s stationary points stay in place. The odd frequency pattern follows from the two endpoint conditions, rather than an arbitrary decision to omit even frequencies.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes
teaching: Air has **inertia**, so moving air tends to keep moving. Compression produces a restoring effect, represented by the model’s spring-like links. The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube, rather than traveling steadily from the glottis to the lips.

The glottal end is treated as fixed and the open lips as free. **Mode 1 is F1-like**, the lowest resonance pattern; **Mode 2 is F2-like**, with another internal reversal. In the ideal uniform reference, Mode 2 repeats three times as fast. A changed tract shape can alter that simple relationship.

A resonance pattern describes the air system’s coordinated back-and-forth movement. F1 and F2 do not identify two separate streams or two positions from which sound is emitted. At one location, neighboring elements may move together while their gaps hardly change. At another, the gaps may repeatedly close and open. A constriction acts on both modes at the same physical place, but their different movement and compression patterns give the changed region a different role in each.

The /a/ marker is about one-third of the distance from the glottis, /i/ about two-thirds, and /u/ at the lips. Each marks the same place in both modes. Added mass matters where a mode moves strongly; increased springiness matters where it compresses strongly. Comparing these local roles explains why one narrowing can affect F1 and F2 differently.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression
teaching: **Movement** is how far an air element travels. **Compression** is how much the spacing between neighbors changes. Several elements can travel together while their gaps remain nearly constant. Elsewhere, gaps close and open strongly near a point with little movement of its own.

Follow one circle through a cycle to see movement. Compare neighboring gaps to see compressed and more spread-out regions. Changing compression supplies a spring-like restoring effect, while the air’s inertia keeps it moving.

The closed end restricts movement and the open end permits it. Higher modes place their alternating regions differently within the same tube. The moving Schwa reference and **F1, F2, and F3** rows describe resonances of one air system. A constriction can strongly affect moving mass in one mode and compression in another, so its effect depends on the mode as well as its location.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode
teaching: Follow a marked location through a complete cycle. Watching its air element reveals how far it moves; comparing its neighbors reveals changes in spacing. A single still frame cannot establish whether that location usually has large movement or strong compression changes.

Where movement is strong, greater **effective mass** makes the air harder to speed up and reverse. The cycle takes longer, tending to lower the resonance. Where compression changes strongly, greater **stiffness** produces a stronger return toward usual spacing. When that effect dominates, the cycle becomes faster and the resonance rises.

**Modes 1, 2, and 3** arrange these regions differently. Predicting a local change therefore requires identifying both the position and the mode. The same physical location can strongly involve movement in one pattern and compression in another.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed
teaching: **Tongue height** and **front–back position** describe vowel articulation. The vowel in **dean** is high and front, with its marked narrowing about two-thirds of the way from the glottis to the lips. **Dune** is high and back, with a highlighted narrowing at the lips. Sharing tongue height does not give them the same tract shape.

**Dan** is low and front; **Don** is low and back, with its narrowing marked about one-third of the distance from the glottis. **Done** is central and labeled “No constriction,” providing the relatively unconstricted reference. Dan has no numbered narrowing position.

The labels describe related but different features. High versus low concerns tongue height; front versus back concerns its position along the mouth; the marked fraction concerns distance along the air path. A shared label such as high therefore leaves other shape differences open. Dean and dune can both be high while narrowing different places, and those places can play different roles in the second resonance pattern. Describing articulation identifies what changed physically; comparing the air modes explains what that change does to the sound.

These fractions locate changes along the air passage, starting at the glottis. A narrowing changes the local mass-like and spring-like effects. Its acoustic consequence depends on how each mode moves and compresses that region, connecting vowel shape with the direction of a formant change.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness
teaching: A **constriction** narrows the air passage. In the lecture’s account, bunching air increases its local density and mass-like effect. Compression also increases resistance to further compression, producing a stronger spring-like effect.

The **mass effect** matters where the air moves strongly. A greater moving load is harder to turn around, tending to lower frequency. The **stiffness effect** matters where the air compresses and expands strongly. A stronger return toward usual spacing makes the vibration faster, tending to raise frequency.

To distinguish the two effects, follow one air element and then compare it with its neighbors through the cycle. Its travel shows the movement involved in carrying the local load. The closing and opening gaps show compression and the restoring response. Neither a tongue-height label nor one frozen frame gives both pieces of information. The constriction’s position identifies where the properties changed, and the mode’s movement identifies how that change contributes to the particular resonance being considered.

These effects do not automatically cancel. Neighbors can move together with little spacing change, or compress strongly near a point with little movement. Each mode places these regions differently. The same narrowing can therefore act mainly through mass for one formant and mainly through stiffness for another, explaining opposite frequency changes without reversing either physical rule.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location
teaching: **Mode 1 and Mode 2** belong to the same air column, with a constrained glottal end and open lips. Both move strongly near the lips, but Mode 2 has an additional internal reversal and a different arrangement of movement and compression.

The back, front, and lip markers identify the same physical places in both patterns. A narrowing at one marker changes that region for both modes. Strong movement makes its mass-like effect important, tending to slow the vibration. Strong compression makes its spring-like effect important, tending to speed it.

This explains why one narrowing can move **F1 and F2** in different directions. The three-times frequency relation belongs to the ideal uniform reference. Formants are tract resonances that can change with tract shape; they are different from source harmonics, whose spacing comes from vocal-fold repetition.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model
teaching: The **/u/ model** adds loading near the open lips, the free end of the air column. Both the F1-like and F2-like patterns have substantial movement there. The enlarged elements represent greater **effective mass**, not heavier individual air molecules.

More moving mass is harder to speed up and reverse. Where this effect dominates, each cycle takes longer and frequency falls. Because both modes move strongly near the lips, the result is **F1 down and F2 down** relative to the uniform reference.

The two rows make it possible to compare the same lip location across different resonance patterns. Both have strong movement there, even though their internal arrangements differ. Increasing the load therefore slows both without requiring that their shapes or frequencies become identical. F1 remains the lower resonance and F2 the next one. The important comparison is the direction of each change relative to its own uniform reference, not whether the two frequencies have become equal or whether all parts of the tract move equally.

The shared direction follows from the changed location’s role in both patterns. It is not a rule that every constriction lowers every resonance. The air continues moving back and forth around its usual positions; the larger elements identify the load involved in that movement.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The **/i/ constriction** lies near the front, about two-thirds of the way from the glottis to the lips. It changes the same physical region in both modes, but that region contributes differently to their movement and compression.

For **Mode 1**, movement makes the **mass effect** more important. The extra effective load is harder to reverse, slowing the cycle and lowering F1. For **Mode 2**, compression makes the **springiness effect** more important. A stronger restoring response speeds the cycle and raises F2.

The marked region is not moved to a new location when the mode changes. What changes is the role of that same region within the coordinated movement. Neighbors moving together make extra moving load important; neighbors repeatedly approaching and separating make the restoring response important. Comparing both rows prevents the narrowing from being treated as a single instruction to raise or lower every frequency. The two arrows summarize separate causal explanations, one involving slower movement of added mass and the other a faster return from compression.

The result is **lower F1 and higher F2** relative to the uniform reference. Increasing mass-like and spring-like effects together does not mean they cancel. Their importance depends on how each mode uses the narrowed region, so one constriction can move the two resonances in opposite directions.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern
teaching: The **/a/ constriction** lies farther back, about one-third of the way from the glottis to the lips. This changes a different part of each mode from the front /i/ narrowing, while the basic effects of mass and stiffness remain the same.

For **Mode 1**, compression is important at the changed region. Greater springiness supplies a stronger restoring response, making the cycle faster and raising F1. For **Mode 2**, movement matters more there. Greater effective mass makes the moving air harder to reverse, slowing the cycle and lowering F2.

The narrowing affects the same back location in both rows, but the rows describe different coordinated movements of the air. A region can have little movement of its own while its neighbors repeatedly squeeze together and spread apart. It can also move strongly with relatively little spacing change. Those two roles explain why the spring-like effect dominates the first mode here while the moving-load effect dominates the second. Changing constriction location changes which role is most important; it does not change what mass or stiffness means.

The result is **higher F1 and lower F2**, reversing the /i/ pattern. The explanation connects constriction location with local movement or compression, then with the effect on frequency. The directions describe the model’s predicted change rather than numerical measurements of its size.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes
teaching: **Air movement** concerns how far an element travels; **compression** concerns changes in the gaps between neighbors. Elements can travel together with little change in spacing. Elsewhere, neighbors can approach and separate strongly around a point whose own movement is small. Smaller gaps mean compression, while wider gaps mean rarefaction, or more spread-out air.

The moving **Schwa** row supplies the uniform-tube reference. The F1, F2, and F3 rows separate resonance patterns of that same air column. The closed left end restricts movement and the open right end allows it. Higher modes fit more alternating regions of movement and compression into the tube.

Compression changes supply a restoring response because crowded air pushes back toward its usual spacing. The moving air also has inertia, so it continues moving as that restoring response changes. Together they support repeated motion around the usual positions. A region with large movement can carry substantial moving mass without being the region that squeezes most strongly. A region with large spacing changes can supply strong restoring action without its central element traveling far. These observations connect the visible circles and gaps with the mass-and-spring explanation.

Following an element over a cycle reveals movement; following neighboring gaps reveals compression. Added mass matters most where movement is strong, while added stiffness matters most where compression changes strongly. These locations differ between modes. The rows represent different resonances, not separate air streams.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing
teaching: The vocal folds supply the voiced **source**. **F0** is its repetition rate and sets the spacing between harmonic components. The 100, 250, and 350 Hz examples spread the harmonic lines progressively farther apart, leaving fewer components in the same frequency window.

The comparison links heavier, looser folds with slower repetition and lighter, tighter folds with faster repetition. Mass resists changes in movement, while restoring action brings the folds back. The membrane illustration separates patterns and combines their movements; its harmonic frequencies are assigned, rather than a general result about all natural membranes.

A voiced vowel contains **multiple frequencies**. Source repetition determines the available harmonics. The vocal tract then strengthens some regions and weakens others. Changing pitch therefore changes source spacing, while changing vowel shape changes the tract’s favored regions. These are distinct contributions to the same sound.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics
teaching: The **vocal-tract filter** changes the relative strengths of harmonics supplied by the source. Its resonances, or **formants**, favor nearby components. Changing the tongue and lips changes these favored frequency regions.

Schwa has separated first and second resonances. The /u/ filter places both lower and also marks a third. The front /i/ or /I/ example has low F1 and much higher F2. The /a/ drawing places its first two targets close together at **800 and 900 Hz**. Those values belong to this particular illustration.

A formant target identifies a tract resonance; a harmonic line identifies a source component. The target can lie between source lines and still strengthen nearby harmonics. Filtering changes their heights without requiring a new component exactly at each target. Source spacing and the filter’s pattern are therefore different properties.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches
teaching: Within a **vowel column**, the filter stays fixed while F0 changes. Across a row, harmonic spacing stays fixed while the vowel filter changes. These comparisons separate effects of the source from effects of tract shape.

Low F0 puts many harmonics near each resonance. Their heights describe the filter’s **envelope**, the smooth pattern of favored strengths. Higher F0 leaves wider gaps and fewer samples. A strong line may lie beside a formant target rather than exactly on it, even though the target has not moved.

The nearby /a/ targets can consequently look like one grouped region. Closer harmonics provide more information without guaranteeing two visibly separate peaks. Difficulty reading them does not establish that a resonance disappeared. A line’s horizontal position gives frequency and its height gives strength; unchanged targets with wider-spaced lines indicate a source change.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram
teaching: A **spectrum** gives frequency horizontally and amplitude by peak height for one short slice of sound. The sequence contains three /i/ slices followed by three /a/ slices. A **spectrogram** places those slices from left to right through time, with frequency running upward.

Peak amplitude becomes **darkness**: black is high, gray medium, and white low. A rising band moves to a higher frequency; a darkening band becomes stronger at its present frequency. Moving right in a spectrum means higher frequency, while moving right in the spectrogram means later time.

During the **/i/ to /a/** transition, the first strong band rises and the second falls. One upper band also moves downward while a fainter band remains in the higher-frequency region. Connecting adjacent slices traces the changing resonance pattern. Position and darkness carry different information about that change.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Speech-complexity experiment prompt
Use formants as input to vowel recognition
teaching: **F1 and F2** describe the first two resonance regions emphasized by the vocal tract. They provide a compact pair of sound measurements for the vowel-recognition task, rather than every individual point in the waveform.

The **input** gives measurements; the intended **output** distinguishes candidate vowel categories. These are different kinds of information. Knowing the formant pair supplies evidence about the sound, while knowing the true label tells which category that example belongs to. Recognition requires relating the measured pattern to the category.

The proposed exercise trains a network with students’ formant measurements, connecting the physical explanation of speech with AI. This establishes the inputs and task. Demonstrating successful recognition would require results from training and testing, which are not supplied by the proposal itself.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network
teaching: The network receives **two inputs, F1 and F2**, whose order preserves their meanings. In a **fully connected layer**, every receiving neuron connects to every neuron in the previous layer. Each connection has a weight. The receiving neuron multiplies each incoming value by its weight and adds the products.

The hidden layers contain **three, two, and four neurons**, followed by five outputs. Hidden values are intermediate combinations, not new measured formants or already-correct categories. Different weights let neurons combine the same inputs differently.

From top to bottom, the outputs correspond to **/done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/, and /Dan/**. Keeping that order preserves the meaning of each value. The layers are **purely linear**, with no activation function between their weighted sums. Passing these sums onward describes the computation, but does not itself ensure that the final values are probabilities.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections
teaching: The input example gives **F1 as 320 and F2 as 2000**. Inputs are measurements of the sound; **weights** are settings that determine how the network combines those measurements. Changing weights can change internal results even when the input pair stays fixed.

Each connection supplies one weight. A neuron multiplies its incoming values by their weights and adds the products. A neuron receiving F1 and F2 therefore has two incoming weights, while the three receiving neurons can form different combinations of that same pair. The heading says **blue positive and orange negative**, but negative labels are green in the rendered figure. Use the written signs to identify direction and the sizes to identify strength. Contributions can reinforce or oppose one another.

The displayed weights are **random starting values**, not learned vowel knowledge. A **forward pass** processes an example using the current weights. **Learning** changes those settings. Naming the outputs does not prove that the initial network recognizes their categories correctly.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution
teaching: A **forward pass** carries the formant information through the layers using their current weights. Each layer combines values from the previous one. This produces an output; learning would additionally change the weights.

The illustrated distribution assigns **0.5 to /done/, 0.2 to /Dan/, and 0.1 to each other candidate**. /done/ is therefore the favored prediction. The alternatives retain some support. Valid probabilities lie between zero and one and add to one. These bars satisfy that condition, but the purely linear code lacks a step ensuring such a distribution, so they illustrate an intended output rather than a verified result of the shown weights.

The **predicted category** is the one favored by the model. The **true category** is the example’s actual label. Judging correctness requires that true label; the largest bar and reaction symbol alone do not supply it.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch
teaching: The code imports **torch** and its neural-network tools as **nn**, then assigns the model to **net**. **nn.Sequential** puts its layers in the order information passes through them. Each **nn.Linear** produces weighted sums from incoming values.

In **nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False)**, two inputs feed three receiving neurons. The remaining layers change three values to two, two to four, and four to five. Each output count matches the next layer’s input count, allowing information to pass through the sequence. The final five values correspond to the five candidate labels.

Every incoming connection keeps its weight. **bias=False** removes an extra constant added to a weighted sum, rather than removing weights or preventing learning. No activation layers appear, so the sequence remains linear. Declaring this structure does not train it or compute the illustrated probability bars; training would require examples and a process for changing weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network
teaching: **F1 and F2** are the two formant measurements supplied to the network. The five output positions stand for **done, dune, dean, Don, and Dan**, in that order. The network receives measurements of the sound and produces a response for each possible word. The input positions and output positions therefore have different jobs, even though both are drawn as circles.

Between the inputs and outputs are three **hidden layers**, containing three, two, and four neurons. A hidden neuron receives values from the layer before it and sends its result onward. The arrangement is **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**. These numbers count the units in successive layers. They do not count recordings or training trials.

**Fully connected** means that every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each connection has its own **weight**, which controls how the value traveling along that connection contributes to the receiving neuron. A positive weight preserves the sign of its contribution, while a negative weight reverses it. The receiving neuron combines all its incoming contributions. The same input can affect several hidden neurons because its outgoing connections carry different weights. F1 contributes to all three neurons in the first hidden layer, but it is not multiplied by the same number on every connection. F2 also reaches those three neurons. Each neuron therefore combines the same two measurements in its own way.

The weights are fixed for this network description. Changing a formant measurement changes what travels through the connections. Changing a weight changes how strongly a connection contributes. Those are different changes to the system. A connection weight specifies how a value contributes to a receiving neuron, rather than giving the probability of an individual word.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs
teaching: **Forward propagation** carries information from the inputs through the hidden layers to the outputs. F1 is **320** and F2 is **2000**. For the top neuron in the first hidden layer, each input is multiplied by its connection weight, and the two products are added. The positive contribution from F1 and the negative contribution from F2 combine to give **−0.40**.

This multiplication followed by addition is an **inner product**. The other two neurons receive the same formants through different weights, so their results are **6.64** and **2.72**. A negative result is still a value that the next layer can use. It does not mean that the neuron or its connections have disappeared.

Each later layer repeats the same operation using the values from the layer immediately before it. The next pair is approximately **5.50 and −5.93**. Those two values then produce four hidden values, approximately **1.57, −1.95, −1.95, and −2.88**. Information moves through the layers in that order because a later neuron requires the earlier neurons’ results. The five final weighted sums are **logits**, or scores before they become probabilities. **Softmax** exponentiates each score and divides it by the sum of the exponentiated scores. The resulting probabilities share one total. A negative logit can therefore lead to a positive probability, and a positive hidden value is not itself a probability.

**Done** receives the largest probability, about **55.7%**, while **dean** receives about **8.1%**. These are the network’s current responses to this input. They do not establish the true word. The hidden activations here are linear, the weights stay fixed during the forward pass, and the calculations retain more precision than the rounded labels.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target
teaching: The **computed output** is the network’s current probability distribution. The **desired output** identifies **dean** with a 1 and gives the other four words a 0. This target says which word belongs to the recording. It does not describe the probabilities the untrained network already produces, so the largest computed response can disagree with the desired word.

**Cross-entropy loss** measures the mismatch using the probability assigned to the true word. Dean currently receives only about **8.1%**. Assigning more probability to dean reduces this loss, while assigning it less increases the loss. The target and computed output therefore supply the information needed to evaluate how the weights contribute to the mistake.

**Backpropagation** works backward from the output connections toward the input connections. The final layer’s contribution to the loss is found first. That information is then used to determine how the preceding hidden layers contributed. The calculation proceeds from the output connections to the connections into hidden layer 3, hidden layer 2, and finally hidden layer 1. A **gradient** describes how the loss changes with a small change in a weight. The update subtracts the learning rate times that gradient from the old weight. A positive gradient leads to a decrease in that weight, and a negative gradient leads to an increase. Learning therefore does not mean making every positive connection larger or every negative connection smaller.

The activations and probabilities stored from the forward pass stay fixed throughout the backward calculation. All gradients use the original weights and stored activations, so they belong to one simultaneous parameter update. A new forward pass would be required to obtain the updated network’s predictions. The input connections use a smaller learning rate because their inputs are raw formant values in hertz.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error
teaching: Increasing a weight changes its contribution to the receiving neuron, but its effect on **error** depends on what that contribution eventually does to the outputs. The desired word is **dean**, while the network currently gives its largest probability to **done**. The relevant question is how a small weight change affects the probability assigned to the true word.

The pink-marked positive connection runs from the top neuron in the last hidden layer to **done**. That hidden neuron has a positive activation, approximately **1.57**. Increasing this weight raises done’s final score. Because softmax makes the five output probabilities share one total, strengthening this incorrect candidate reduces the probability available to dean and increases the cross-entropy loss.

The blue-marked first connection runs from **F1** to the top neuron in the first hidden layer. Increasing that weight raises the first hidden neuron’s value because F1 is positive. Its influence then passes through several positive and negative connections and reaches several outputs. The effect on the final error cannot be decided from the sign of this first connection alone.

For the supplied network and dean target, the full backward calculation gives a positive gradient for this input connection too. A small increase therefore raises the error here, while the update decreases the weight. The two marked connections both call for decreases in this example, but the early connection requires the combined influence of the downstream paths to establish that direction.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations
teaching: The **last weights**, labeled **W5**, directly determine the final output scores from the last hidden activations. Their effects on the error are close to the output comparison. Once the computed and desired outputs are available, the contribution of these final connections can be found without tracing another hidden layer beyond them.

The **first weights**, labeled **W2**, affect the first hidden activations. Those activations affect two more hidden layers before the output scores are produced. An early weight’s contribution to error therefore includes what the later weights do with the values it changes. Its effect is distributed across the paths that continue from it.

**Backpropagation** calculates the effects near the output first and reuses them when working toward earlier layers. The downstream part of an early connection’s effect has already been computed. It can be combined with the local connection information instead of repeatedly solving the entire downstream calculation separately for every early weight. This reuse is the connection to **Bellman–Viterbi dynamic programming**. Smaller dependent calculations are solved and their results are retained for the calculations that depend on them. Working backward fits the dependence of the error on the layers, because the effect of an early layer includes the layers after it.

**SGD** supplies the weight-adjustment rule, while backpropagation efficiently supplies the gradients that rule uses. Combining **SGD with dynamic programming** connects these two jobs. The backward calculation determines how the error depends on the weights, and the optimizer uses those results to change the weights.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row
teaching: The **Formant_Inputs** matrix has **110 rows and two columns**. Each row contains F1 and F2 for one recording, so the columns represent the two sound measurements rather than two possible words. The network processes the two values from a row together as one example.

The **TrueVowel_Outputs** matrix has **110 rows and five columns**. Its columns are **done, dune, dean, Don, and Dan**. The row for a recording puts a 1 in the correct word’s position and 0 in the other four positions. This is a **one-hot target**, because one position identifies the category.

The rows in the two matrices must stay matched. The third input row contains **320 and 2000**, and the third target row identifies **dean**. Moving one input row without moving its matching target would pair the sound measurements with the wrong answer. Keeping the same number of rows is not sufficient if their order no longer agrees. The complete matrices contain 110 examples in paired rows. The five listed examples identify the column arrangement rather than supplying all 110 recordings. The five target columns describe the available categories. They do not mean that each recording supplies five separate input examples.

The network’s current output is distinct from this target matrix. It assigns its own probabilities to the five words, with done currently highest for the dean example. The target records the correct label even when the network makes a mistake. Training compares those two kinds of information rather than replacing the target with the network’s strongest response.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch
teaching: **X** contains the two formant values for each of the 110 recordings, and **Y** contains the five-position targets for the same recordings. **torch.load** loads the saved tensor files, and **.float()** supplies floating-point values. The program assumes these files already exist with the stated shapes. It does not create the recordings or their labels.

**nn.Sequential** connects the layers in their written order. **nn.Linear(2, 3)** maps each pair of inputs into three values. The later layers map three to two, two to four, and four to five. These dimensions preserve the **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** arrangement. There is no sigmoid declared between these hidden layers.

**SGD** is given the network’s parameters and a **learning rate of 0.1**. **zero_grad()** clears previously stored gradients. **net(X)** performs the forward calculation, and **CrossEntropyLoss** compares the final scores with Y. This loss handles the softmax-related calculation internally, so the final linear layer supplies logits rather than a separately declared softmax output. **loss.backward()** computes the gradients of the loss with respect to the parameters. **sgd.step()** then changes those parameters using the gradients. These are separate operations. Computing how a weight affects the error does not by itself change that weight, and clearing gradients does not erase the learned parameter values.

All **110 rows** contribute to this one gradient step. The code has no repeated training loop. It also uses PyTorch’s default linear-layer initialization and bias options, whereas the numerical drawing uses hand-selected weights with no biases. The code specifies the same layer sizes, but it does not automatically reproduce the displayed numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation
teaching: The **sigmoid activation function** takes an inner product as its input and returns a value between 0 and 1. A large negative input produces an activation near 0, and a large positive input produces one near 1. The S-shaped relationship is gradual rather than an exact switch that returns only two possible values.

The horizontal coordinate is **linear activation**, the weighted sum before sigmoid, and the vertical coordinate is **sigmoid activation**. An input of **−4** gives about **0.0180**, whereas an input of **4** gives about **0.9820**. Around the center the curve is steep. Near the upper and lower ends it flattens, so further input changes produce relatively small output changes.

The formula divides 1 by 1 plus the exponential of the negative input. Moving the input toward larger positive values makes that denominator approach 1, so the output approaches 1. Moving it toward larger negative values enlarges the denominator, so the output approaches 0. The weighted sum is transformed rather than simply passed on unchanged. Physical differences can be compressed or emphasized by this input–activation relationship. Distinct inputs near a flat end give similar activations, while inputs on different sides of the steep central region can produce much more different activations. Similarity in the incoming measurements therefore does not translate into an equal-sized difference at every point in the response.

**Edgar Adrian** supplies biological context through work on nerve activity, including the 1932 Nobel Prize. The mathematical sigmoid is a model of graded activation. Adrian’s rate-coding work concerns changes in firing rate, so a bounded model activation should not be confused with the claim that biological neurons can only have two possible firing rates.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity
teaching: The inputs remain **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**, and the connection weights stay fixed. Sigmoid is added to the **nine hidden neurons**, one neuron at a time, in the order of three neurons in the first hidden layer, two in the second, and four in the third. Purple neurons remain linear, while green neurons pass their inner product through sigmoid.

The first hidden neuron changes from **−0.400** to about **0.401**. Its new output changes what the next layer receives, so all downstream values are recalculated. The process is not a matter of putting sigmoid around every number stored from the all-linear network. Once an earlier output changes, the later weighted sums change as well.

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network
teaching: **F1 and F2** are the two formant measurements supplied to the network. The five output positions stand for **done, dune, dean, Don, and Dan**, in that order. The network receives measurements of the sound and produces a response for each possible word. The input positions and output positions therefore have different jobs, even though both are drawn as circles.

Between the inputs and outputs are three **hidden layers**, containing three, two, and four neurons. A hidden neuron receives values from the layer before it and sends its result onward. The arrangement is **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5**. These numbers count the units in successive layers. They do not count recordings or training trials.

**Fully connected** means that every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next layer. Each connection has its own **weight**, which controls how the value traveling along that connection contributes to the receiving neuron. A positive weight preserves the sign of its contribution, while a negative weight reverses it. The receiving neuron combines all its incoming contributions. The same input can affect several hidden neurons because its outgoing connections carry different weights. F1 contributes to all three neurons in the first hidden layer, but it is not multiplied by the same number on every connection. F2 also reaches those three neurons. Each neuron therefore combines the same two measurements in its own way.

The weights are fixed for this network description. Changing a formant measurement changes what travels through the connections. Changing a weight changes how strongly a connection contributes. Those are different changes to the system. A connection weight specifies how a value contributes to a receiving neuron, rather than giving the probability of an individual word.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs
teaching: **Forward propagation** carries information from the inputs through the hidden layers to the outputs. F1 is **320** and F2 is **2000**. For the top neuron in the first hidden layer, each input is multiplied by its connection weight, and the two products are added. The positive contribution from F1 and the negative contribution from F2 combine to give **−0.40**.

This multiplication followed by addition is an **inner product**. The other two neurons receive the same formants through different weights, so their results are **6.64** and **2.72**. A negative result is still a value that the next layer can use. It does not mean that the neuron or its connections have disappeared.

Each later layer repeats the same operation using the values from the layer immediately before it. The next pair is approximately **5.50 and −5.93**. Those two values then produce four hidden values, approximately **1.57, −1.95, −1.95, and −2.88**. Information moves through the layers in that order because a later neuron requires the earlier neurons’ results. The five final weighted sums are **logits**, or scores before they become probabilities. **Softmax** exponentiates each score and divides it by the sum of the exponentiated scores. The resulting probabilities share one total. A negative logit can therefore lead to a positive probability, and a positive hidden value is not itself a probability.

**Done** receives the largest probability, about **55.7%**, while **dean** receives about **8.1%**. These are the network’s current responses to this input. They do not establish the true word. The hidden activations here are linear, the weights stay fixed during the forward pass, and the calculations retain more precision than the rounded labels.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Vowel formants overlap across five categories
teaching: The scatterplot shows every measurement in the vowel data, **525 observations** with **105 tokens of each vowel**. Each dot is one recorded vowel. **F1** runs along the horizontal axis and **F2** along the vertical axis, both in hertz. The color says which word the recording belongs to, so the plot shows the same kind of input the network receives, two formant numbers, together with the correct answer for each one.

The five categories match the network’s five outputs. Red is **i (dean)**, magenta is **ae (Dan)**, blue is **u (dune)**, cyan is **a (Don)**, and green is **schwa (done)**. Each category forms a cloud rather than a single point, because the same vowel comes out with different formants from token to token. Nothing was removed from the data, so the occasional dot far from its cloud stays in the plot.

Some vowels are easy to pick out. The red **i** tokens sit high on the F2 axis, mostly above about 2000 Hz, with a low F1. The magenta **ae** tokens spread toward high F1 values, out past 800 Hz. Those two clouds are separated from most of the others by where they fall on one or both axes. The other three overlap heavily. The blue **u**, cyan **a**, and green **schwa** tokens crowd into the lower middle of the plot, roughly between 300 and 800 Hz in F1 and between 800 and 1600 Hz in F2. A point in that region could belong to any of the three. Two formant numbers alone do not separate these vowels cleanly.

This overlap matters for every network trained on these data. A classifier sees only F1 and F2, so tokens that sit in the same place on the plot look the same to it, whatever their true label. The overlap sets a limit on how many tokens any decision rule based on these two numbers can label correctly, which helps explain why networks trained on these data do not come close to perfect accuracy.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target
teaching: The **computed output** is the network’s current probability distribution. The **desired output** identifies **dean** with a 1 and gives the other four words a 0. This target says which word belongs to the recording. It does not describe the probabilities the untrained network already produces, so the largest computed response can disagree with the desired word.

**Cross-entropy loss** measures the mismatch using the probability assigned to the true word. Dean currently receives only about **8.1%**. Assigning more probability to dean reduces this loss, while assigning it less increases the loss. The target and computed output therefore supply the information needed to evaluate how the weights contribute to the mistake.

**Backpropagation** works backward from the output connections toward the input connections. The final layer’s contribution to the loss is found first. That information is then used to determine how the preceding hidden layers contributed. The calculation proceeds from the output connections to the connections into hidden layer 3, hidden layer 2, and finally hidden layer 1. A **gradient** describes how the loss changes with a small change in a weight. The update subtracts the learning rate times that gradient from the old weight. A positive gradient leads to a decrease in that weight, and a negative gradient leads to an increase. Learning therefore does not mean making every positive connection larger or every negative connection smaller.

The activations and probabilities stored from the forward pass stay fixed throughout the backward calculation. All gradients use the original weights and stored activations, so they belong to one simultaneous parameter update. A new forward pass would be required to obtain the updated network’s predictions. The input connections use a smaller learning rate because their inputs are raw formant values in hertz.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error
teaching: Increasing a weight changes its contribution to the receiving neuron, but its effect on **error** depends on what that contribution eventually does to the outputs. The desired word is **dean**, while the network currently gives its largest probability to **done**. The relevant question is how a small weight change affects the probability assigned to the true word.

The pink-marked positive connection runs from the top neuron in the last hidden layer to **done**. That hidden neuron has a positive activation, approximately **1.57**. Increasing this weight raises done’s final score. Because softmax makes the five output probabilities share one total, strengthening this incorrect candidate reduces the probability available to dean and increases the cross-entropy loss.

The blue-marked first connection runs from **F1** to the top neuron in the first hidden layer. Increasing that weight raises the first hidden neuron’s value because F1 is positive. Its influence then passes through several positive and negative connections and reaches several outputs. The effect on the final error cannot be decided from the sign of this first connection alone.

For the supplied network and dean target, the full backward calculation gives a positive gradient for this input connection too. A small increase therefore raises the error here, while the update decreases the weight. The two marked connections both call for decreases in this example, but the early connection requires the combined influence of the downstream paths to establish that direction.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations
teaching: The **last weights**, labeled **W5**, directly determine the final output scores from the last hidden activations. Their effects on the error are close to the output comparison. Once the computed and desired outputs are available, the contribution of these final connections can be found without tracing another hidden layer beyond them.

The **first weights**, labeled **W2**, affect the first hidden activations. Those activations affect two more hidden layers before the output scores are produced. An early weight’s contribution to error therefore includes what the later weights do with the values it changes. Its effect is distributed across the paths that continue from it.

**Backpropagation** calculates the effects near the output first and reuses them when working toward earlier layers. The downstream part of an early connection’s effect has already been computed. It can be combined with the local connection information instead of repeatedly solving the entire downstream calculation separately for every early weight. This reuse is the connection to **Bellman–Viterbi dynamic programming**. Smaller dependent calculations are solved and their results are retained for the calculations that depend on them. Working backward fits the dependence of the error on the layers, because the effect of an early layer includes the layers after it.

**SGD** supplies the weight-adjustment rule, while backpropagation efficiently supplies the gradients that rule uses. Combining **SGD with dynamic programming** connects these two jobs. The backward calculation determines how the error depends on the weights, and the optimizer uses those results to change the weights.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation
teaching: The **sigmoid activation function** takes an inner product as its input and returns a value between 0 and 1. A large negative input produces an activation near 0, and a large positive input produces one near 1. The S-shaped relationship is gradual rather than an exact switch that returns only two possible values.

The horizontal coordinate is **linear activation**, the weighted sum before sigmoid, and the vertical coordinate is **sigmoid activation**. An input of **−4** gives about **0.0180**, whereas an input of **4** gives about **0.9820**. Around the center the curve is steep. Near the upper and lower ends it flattens, so further input changes produce relatively small output changes.

The formula divides 1 by 1 plus the exponential of the negative input. Moving the input toward larger positive values makes that denominator approach 1, so the output approaches 1. Moving it toward larger negative values enlarges the denominator, so the output approaches 0. The weighted sum is transformed rather than simply passed on unchanged. Physical differences can be compressed or emphasized by this input–activation relationship. Distinct inputs near a flat end give similar activations, while inputs on different sides of the steep central region can produce much more different activations. Similarity in the incoming measurements therefore does not translate into an equal-sized difference at every point in the response.

**Edgar Adrian** supplies biological context through work on nerve activity, including the 1932 Nobel Prize. The mathematical sigmoid is a model of graded activation. Adrian’s rate-coding work concerns changes in firing rate, so a bounded model activation should not be confused with the claim that biological neurons can only have two possible firing rates.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates
teaching: The code trains the same **2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5** network on the vowel data. Every layer is **nn.Linear with bias=False**, and there are no activations between them, so the network is the all-linear one from the earlier forward-propagation example. **torch.manual_seed(0)** fixes the random starting weights, so the run starts from one particular **initialization**. The formants are divided by 1000, converting hertz to kilohertz, which keeps the input numbers small.

The targets are one-hot rows, and **argmax(1)** turns each row into the number of its correct class for checking accuracy. The loss is **CrossEntropyLoss**, and the optimizer is plain **SGD** with a **learning rate of 0.1**. The loop runs **2,000 epochs**. In each one it clears old gradients, computes the loss for all the examples at once, backpropagates, and takes one step, so every epoch is one **full-batch update**.

After each update, the code measures accuracy without computing gradients. For each token the largest of the five scores is the network’s answer, and accuracy is the percentage of tokens where that answer matches the correct class. These are the same **525 training examples** the network learns from, so this is **training accuracy**, not a test on new recordings. The curve starts at about **20%**, which is what labeling everything as one of five equally common vowels would give. It stays flat for about the first 200 updates, then climbs quickly into the 40s. Near update 390 it drops sharply back toward 20% for a moment, then recovers and settles near 45%. After about 450 updates it barely changes. The final training accuracy is **44.95%**, which is 236 of the 525 tokens.

The note under the code explains where the curve comes from. PyTorch was not available where the plot was made, so the plotted run comes from an equivalent **NumPy** implementation of the same network, loss, scaling, learning rate and number of updates. The code shows the PyTorch version of the procedure, and the curve shows what that procedure did when it was run.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy
teaching: The same training procedure is run ten times with **seeds 0 through 9**. Each run builds a fresh model and a fresh SGD optimizer, so the only thing that changes from run to run is the **initialization**, the random starting weights. The data, the scaling, the loss, the learning rate and the 2,000 full-batch updates are identical.

Each colored line is one seed. All ten start near **20%** training accuracy. They differ in when they leave that starting level, some climbing within the first 100 updates and others staying flat for 200 or more. They also differ in their early ups and downs, including short drops back toward 20%, and in the highest accuracy they reach along the way, which is close to 47% for some runs.

Some runs settle within about 350 updates, while the slowest take about 1,000. After that the lines come together and overlap. **All ten finish at 44.95%** training accuracy. Different starting weights send the network down different paths, but every path ends at the same level of performance on these data. The shared final value says that starting the network from a different place did not change how well it could do. Running more seeds or picking the best one would not raise the final accuracy here. The limit comes from the network and the data it is given, the same overlapping vowel clouds, rather than from bad luck in the starting weights.

The note at the bottom repeats that the curves are executed **NumPy** reference runs. Matching seed numbers in NumPy and PyTorch do not produce the same starting weights, so a PyTorch run with seed 3 would not trace exactly the same line as the plotted seed 3.
